messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Carlos, a 67-year-old widowed Latino prosecutor, had built his career on the certainty that he could read people and control any room. That certainty was destroyed during a visit to the home of a long-time friend, a fellow attorney he had trusted for decades. The assault happened in the study, a room Carlos had been in many times, but that afternoon the friend’s young grandchildren were playing in the adjoining living room; Carlos could hear their voices through the half-open door. The friend turned on Carlos without warning, and during the assault Carlos’s cheek pressed against the cold tile floor—a specific, sharp temperature on his skin that he would never forget. Afterwards, he felt irrevocably dirty, as if the contamination had seeped into his bones. The world, he concluded, was fundamentally dangerous, and his body had been permanently damaged, broken in a way that could not be undone.

In the months that followed, the memory of that afternoon became his uninvited companion. It forced its way into his mind with vivid clarity—the children’s laughter, the cold tile, the betrayal—and it always felt as if it were happening right then, not something over and done with. When he walked into a courtroom or a colleague’s office, a familiar face could suddenly trigger that memory, and the moment he heard a child’s voice in a hallway or restaurant, the assault would flood back, along with the unbearable sense of contamination. The cold sensation on his skin, even from a chilly air conditioner, could do the same. Each recurrence of the memory reinforced his belief that the world was a place of hidden threats, and that only constant vigilance could keep him safe.

Carlos began to change his daily habits in subtle but profound ways. As a prosecutor, he had to enter many new rooms—witness waiting areas, unfamiliar courtrooms, deposition suites. But now he avoided going to any place he had not already scouted, because he could not assess the danger there. The moment he did enter a room, his eyes automatically swept the space for exits, noting every door and window. He also found himself cataloguing potential weapons in any environment: a letter opener on a desk, a heavy stapler, a lamp cord. This hypervigilance, born from his conviction that danger was everywhere, often triggered his memory of the assault—especially when he spotted an exit that reminded him of the door he had been unable to reach. And the constant scanning itself made him more attuned to triggers: a known person walking toward him would catch his attention, and the cold draft from an air vent would register acutely, each one pulling him back into the traumatic scene.

His negative appraisals deepened the cycle. Feeling contaminated and vulnerable, he was certain that other people—even those he had known for years—carried hidden malice. This belief made him avoid certain colleagues, and he began to see known people not as allies but as potential threats. The more he saw the world as dangerous, the more he stayed away from unfamiliar places, reinforcing his isolation. At the same time, the memory of his physical vulnerability—the sense of being trapped and overpowered—made him scan for weapons even more anxiously. And each time he felt that chill on his skin, it confirmed for him that his body was damaged, which made the memory feel even more present.

One concrete consequence emerged in his work: he requested to be assigned only to cases in courthouses he already knew, and he stopped attending mandatory social gatherings with other attorneys. His supervisors noticed he was declining high-profile assignments that required travel to new venues, and his relationship with his adult daughter suffered because she had young children, and being around them became unbearable. He avoided her home entirely, making excuses.

Carlos finally sought help because the avoidance was no longer sustainable. He had missed a critical court hearing because the assigned room was unfamiliar, and he had spent the morning circling the block, unable to make himself walk in. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never feel clean again, and that his body—the only one he had—had been irreparably broken. But he also hoped that understanding the machinery of his own mind might give him back even a fraction of the control he once had in a courtroom.
